The king threw him from a high tower to the ground, yet he did not die; however, he struck one finger and broke it, which is why it is said that "his finger was broken.
Regarding the phrase "following the teachings of the evil friend Devadatta," it means that he was a close friend of Devadatta and constantly spoke of King Śreṇiya.

The reason this was said is that he approached Ānanda to study the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and practiced the path through the gate of existence; he then claimed to be a Buddha himself.
King Śreṇika believed him and became his patron (*dānapati*).
Bimbisāra was the patron (*dānapati*) of Siddhārtha; thus there were two Buddhas and two patrons.
Devadatta declared:
"I shall remove the former Buddha and become a new Buddha; the King shall remove the former King and become a new King."
King Ajātaśatru accepted his words and immediately imprisoned his father, King Bimbisāra.
Devadatta— here called Tianre (Heavenly Heat)—
was so named because at the time of his birth, there was such intense heat within the chamber that it was a sign of his future rebirth in Avīci Hell.
That person committed three heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), as explained in detail in the *Śāstra* and as analyzed in the Vinaya, and so forth.
Bimbisāra—here translated as "One of Handsome Appearance"—attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
However, regarding the teaching that one person may incur two offenses, an Arhat who kills his own parents incurs two parricides.
Now, since the King, my father, is at the stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna), what offense would be incurred by killing him?
The commentary says:
This seems to be a contradiction.
If that were so, would the killing of one's father be more serious, while the killing of an *ārya* be lighter?

The "Noble One" refers to one who has attained the first fruit [of the path], for while killing one who resembles a father constitutes a semblance of parricide, killing an actual father constitutes true parricide.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the Great Lady of the State," this clarifies the causes and conditions by which the King obtained food and the Dharma, thereby escaping death.
The fine details herein can be understood from the text.

The queen offered parched grain flour, ointments for the body, and garlands, along with vessels filled with juice, to the King; the King then invited Maudgalyāyana to receive the eight precepts on his behalf.
Regarding the statement "Maudgalyāyana is a relative," it is because Maudgalyāyana was of royal lineage and a native of Rājagṛha.

The treatise states: "Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra were close associates; while Śāriputra possessed supreme wisdom, Maudgalyāyana’s family was of noble and distinguished standing, and both resided in Rājagṛha."
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana became a close relative to the king.
The Buddha then dispatched the Venerable Pūrṇa to preach the Dharma to the king.
Due to three causes and conditions, he did not die for twenty-one days.
The lady sent parched grain and drink; the grain was eaten and the drink was drunk, for food and drink sustain the body.
Maudgalyāyana preached the Eight Precepts to him, which he practiced, and Pūrṇa expounded the Dharma, which he understood; practice and understanding sustain the mind.
"For this reason and cause, he did not die for twenty-one days.
From the passage "At that time, Ajātaśatru asked the gatekeeper" onwards is the second section, which clarifies the causes and conditions for holding onto his mother.
As stated in the text.
The reason King Śreṇiya called his father a "thief" was that when he was born, a physiognomist predicted:
"This child shall kill his father."
Because the father wished to kill him, he designated his father as a thief.
If one does not change one's ways regarding major matters, one will instead suffer the resulting chaos.
Jīvaka and the minister Candraprabha cited matters from the Vedas to offer this admonition.
Vidya is also called Vedha; this is translated as "field of knowledge" (vidyā-sthāna).
Jīvaka was the younger half-brother of King Bimbisāra;
thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* refers to him as "my elder brother."
Jīva admonished him, saying:
"Since the beginning of the kalpa, there have been eighteen thousand wicked kings who, out of greed for their kingdoms, murdered their fathers;
yet I have never heard of anyone killing their mother."
This is a well-known instance of loyal remonstrance.
When Daichū (Mahāsammata) first committed an act of rebellion, there were also those who offered counsel.
There was a man named Hyōso (Pṛthu) who remonstrated from above; the details of his remonstrance are as follows.
Mahāprajāpati ultimately refused to accept the admonition and instead cut off her head.
In the present world, even kings may still receive admonitions and subsequently desist; they do not kill their mothers, but rather confine them within the inner palace.
Because they are confined within the deep palace, they are thus able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Through this mindfulness of the Buddha, they are able to behold Śākyamuni and Amitāyus.
This, then, is a matter of great benefit and a skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
If it were not so, there would be no basis for explaining this single sutra.
Now, this is the specific introduction (nidāna) to the sutra.
While the specific introductions of various sutras differ, they can generally be categorized into two types:
First is that which can manifest as a distinct sequence, and second is that which is manifested as a distinct sequence.

Regarding that which can manifest as a distinct sequence: as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, where the heavens rain down four kinds of flowers, the earth quakes in six ways, and a great radiance is emitted—this is the matter of that which can manifest.
The raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth constitute the mental action (manas-karma), while the emission of great radiance constitutes the bodily action (kāya-karma).
This is likewise the case in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, [the Buddha] personally spreads the lion throne and enters the King Samādhi, emitting radiance from his body.
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he proclaims the announcement at dawn, emitting light from the gate of his face.
These constitute the introductory sequence for those who transform others.
As for the introductory sequence for those being transformed, examples include the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* and the *Bhāryā-sūtra*.
In the introduction to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the Elder Ratnākara offered a canopy, whereby the Tathāgata opened the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
The *Bhāryāsūtra* (The Scripture on the Wife) was occasioned by the parents sending a letter.
Because the parents sent a letter, fifteen chapters of scripture could be expounded; this constitutes the specific introduction for the conversion [of the wife].
All the various sūtras do not transcend these two introductory sections.

Now, this present sūtra constitutes a specific introduction for those to be converted; because of this event involving King Śubhavyūha, it expounds the dharma-gate of the causes and effects of the Western Pure Land.
Regarding the specific introductory section concerning those to be converted, there are further two types:
first, auspicious events as the specific introduction; second, inauspicious events as the specific introduction.

As for auspicious events as the specific introduction, this refers to the Elder’s offering of the parasol. The offering of the parasol constitutes material generosity (*āmiṣadāna*); because one attains the opening of the Pure Land through this material generosity, it is thus an auspicious event serving as the specific introduction.

Regarding "evil events" as the specific introduction (*nidāna*), this sutra is so called because King Ajātaśatru harmed his father and took possession of his mother, thereby providing the occasion for the opening of this single sutra; thus, evil events serve as the specific introduction.
However, both the Sūtras and the Vinaya contain these matters; the Sūtras are mostly taught for laypeople, while the Vinaya is taught for monastics.
The Sūtras provide exhortation, whereas the Vinaya provides admonition; thus, they represent the two gates of exhortation and admonition.

As for those who speak of the Vinaya, it was due to the group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus; because of these individuals, from their initial transgressions of the precepts until the final ones, the Tathāgata was able to establish the two hundred and fifty precepts, bringing vast benefit to all sentient beings of the present and the future.

If there were no such person who violates the precepts, the Tathāgata would not have established the prohibitions, and thus there would be no precepts; how then could the benefit of all sentient beings in the present and future be secured, and how could the Buddha-dharma be made to abide for a long time?
That the Buddha-dharma has endured for two thousand years, and even up to ten thousand years, is truly due to the precepts; it is because of them that it has reached the present day.
This is how the group of six bhikṣus acted for the benefit of those who have left the household life, benefiting those who have renounced the world.
If this king were to perform benefits for those living as householders in this present life, he would benefit his fellow householders. Why?

Because I killed my father, the king, out of greed for the throne; I have manifested leprosy in this very body and shall fall into hell. Having already received this "flower-retribution" (the immediate result), the full retribution of hell will soon be upon me.
"O kings and others, do not act in this manner again; such deeds will inevitably bring about evil retribution.
This matter was undertaken solely as a warning to those who commit evil."

Furthermore, wishing to open the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, if he had not harmed the king and seized his mother, there would have been no means by which to reveal the causes and effects of the Pure Land in this sutra.
Moreover, wishing to demonstrate the power of the Great Nirvana, the king’s body fell ill; had he not heard the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he would have fallen into hell seven days hence.
Because he heard this great sutra and performed repentance, his offenses were purified.
To demonstrate the powerful efficacy of the sutra, he harmed his father, the king.
Question:
Although benefiting others later and providing further guidance may seem sufficient, is it not because of the suffering of one's parents?
The explanation says:
Since the Universal Monarch is already a skillful means (*upāya*), and the parents are likewise not real, they are both entirely skillful means.
This need not be discussed.
Nevertheless, speaking in terms of practical matters, it also brings great benefit to one's parents. Why is this?

His father had originally attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, but because he was confined in seclusion, Maudgalyāyana recited the precepts and Pūrṇa expounded the Dharma; consequently, his father reached the stage of *anāgāmin*, attaining the third fruit directly from the first.
If that is so, is this not a great benefit?
Furthermore, as for the mother receiving this benefit: by holding onto her, she comes to recollect the Buddha, sees two Buddhas in the present, and is later reborn in a pure land.
Having already settled his mother in the Pure Land, this is comparable to the worldly practice of providing filial care through material offerings.
As for the fact that he harmed his father, his karma was fixed and could not be altered. Why is this so?
In a former life, King Śreṇya was a seer dwelling in the mountains, while his father, the king, was out hunting and could not find any game.
Seeing the seer, he said:
"I cannot catch anything today; it is surely because of this man."
He then severed the head of the seer.
As the seer was dying, he gave rise to this thought:
"This man has harmed me without cause; I shall harm him without cause."
"Because of this single act of anger, he instead harmed his own father, the king.
Question:
"If the father-king had previously killed a person and ought to have fallen into hell, how could he become a human king?"
The commentary states:
Although he killed the immortal at that time, he subsequently gave rise to fear; through repentance, his transgression was extinguished, and he now attained the status of king.
It is the same for the king of the present age: having killed his father-king, he repented, and thus his transgression was extinguished.
For these reasons, he killed his father and took his mother as his consort.
This precedes the specific introductory section [of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa].
From the passage beginning "At that time, Vaidehī," this text still belongs to the specific introduction.
However, when our late father the King was confined in prison, there was both a stimulus and a response; now that the Queen has been taken captive, there is likewise both a stimulus and a response.
When our late father the King offered his prayers, he moved the holy disciples Maudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa to respond.
Now, when a person prays, they evoke the response of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This explains the meaning of the fourfold formula of resonance and response (*ganying*).
The four phrases are: first, there is resonance but no response; second, there is response but no resonance; third, both response and resonance; and fourth, neither resonance nor response.
It has been said from of old:
"If the pressing stone is swift but one longs for a meeting after five years of separation like the stars Canopus and Sirius, there will be feeling but no response.
If the eastern and western gates of the city appear simultaneously in all ten directions, there is no feeling, yet there is a response."
When Lady Śrīmālā gave rise to this thought, the Buddha appeared in the air;

when Vaidehī prostrated herself in prayer, before she had even raised her head, Śākyamuni was standing before her—this was both a response to her aspiration and a manifestation of her spiritual resonance.
The people of this world are indifferent and do not feel moved toward the Buddha, and the Buddha, in turn, does not respond to them.
Regarding the first two lines, while the facts are evident, the underlying meaning is difficult to understand. Why is this so?
Through response there is retribution, and through retribution there is response.
Given these causes and conditions of response and retribution, how could one see that there is response without retribution, or retribution without response?
It is called "response" (ying) because it awaits "stimulation" (gan), and it is called "stimulation" because it awaits "response.
Since there is no stimulation, how can it be called a response?
One school of interpretation explains:
There are cases where there is no stimulus yet a response occurs, and cases where there is a stimulus yet no response occurs.
This alone constitutes the completion of the explanation. Why is this so?
If there is no stimulus yet there is a response, this means that non-action is used as the stimulus and action is employed as the response.
How can such non-stimulation be achieved?
It is achieved precisely because of the response.
By what means is this responsive manifestation obtained?
It is obtained through the absence of any stimulus.
It is like the old consort in the eastern part of the city; had it not been for her lack of stimulation, she would not have known that the Buddha was manifesting his response.
If there were no response because of the Buddha, one would not know that there is no stimulus.
That there is a response despite the absence of a stimulus is due to the conditions of dependent origination.
However, this "response without a stimulus" contains two meanings:
The first is existence and non-existence; the second is resonance and response.
Regarding existence and non-existence: where there is no resonance yet there is a response, there is the causal condition of non-existence.
This refers to the first of the four propositions: the proposition of "no resonance yet having a response."
As for "resonance" (ganying), it consists of using the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) to resonate and the conditioned (*samskrta*) to respond.
Because there was no resonance from within the city, there arose responses from the ten directions.
Just as there can be response without resonance, so too can there be no response despite the presence of resonance.
This existence and non-existence is, moreover, a matter of stimulus and response.
Why is this? Because there is a stimulus from that [sentient being], there is a Tathāgata; yet, without the stimulus, there would be no response.
For what reason is this so?
It is because there are causes and conditions;
furthermore, there is a further underlying reason.
The reason the Tathāgata did not respond for five years was his desire to cause many roots of goodness to arise in them.
Had he responded in a single thought-moment, those roots of goodness would not have been numerous.

By praying for five years without receiving a response from the Tathāgata, they produced roots of goodness over the course of those five years; thus, there was a response in their own hearts, even though there was no external response from him.
Question:
Since he did not perceive the Buddha for five years, how can he be said to have "perceived" him?
Explanation:
Taking the meaning of "praying for a response over five years," it is termed "response" (*gan*).
Because no [response] was encountered during those five years, it is said that there was "feeling" (*gan*) but no "response" (*ying*).
Now, within these four propositions, this refers to the case where there is feeling but no response.
"Then Vaidehī saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One"—the first chapter concludes here.
Now begins the second part: the actual exposition (*bhāṣya*).
Within this section, there are two combined divisions and four separate ones.
Combined into two parts: first, a general clarification of the Pure Land; second, a specific clarification of the Pure Land.
Divided into four parts, the general and specific sections each open into two: first, the general clarification of the Pure Land, which has two [subdivisions]:
the first is the general inquiry;
Second, the general response.
This also specifically clarifies the Pure Land and consists of two parts:
first, the specific questions; [second, the specific answers].
Next, the specific response.
Although it consists of four sections, they are combined into two chapters—general and specific—in contrast to the preceding introduction.

Within the preceding introduction, there were both the general and specific prefaces; here, in the formal discourse, we have the general clarification of the Pure Land and the specific clarification of the Pure Land.
Now, the first section, which provides a general inquiry regarding the Pure Land, is divided into two parts:
first, the scriptural narrator describes the lady’s appearance and demeanor of sorrowful suffering;
second, she formally speaks to pose her questions.
The beginning is as in the text.
[He] addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what sin in my past lives... and so forth, marks the second section: the formal statement of the inquiry.
Several phrases within this section will be identified as they appear in the text.
"By what sin in my past lives have I given birth to such a wicked son?"—this question concerns the evil causes and conditions of the defiled land, and it has two aspects:
The first question concerns what transgressions he himself committed to have given birth to an evil son; the second question concerns the evil conditions involving Devadatta.
This is not a question of why he was a close friend to the Buddha and Devadatta, but rather a question of for what causes and conditions King Śreṇiya became a close friend to Devadatta.
The Sūtra states, "He is exclusively accompanied by an entourage of evil people"; thus we know that King Ajātaśatru was a close friend of Devadatta.

Regarding the request, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain the place free from sorrow and fear," the former question concerned the defiled land and its evil causes and conditions, whereas this question concerns the causes and conditions of the pure land, as he wishes to depart from evil.
The passage beginning with “not delighting in Jambudvīpa” clarifies the weariness with defilement and the aspiration for purity, expressing the desire for rebirth [in the Pure Land].

Regarding the phrase “now prostrating before the World-Honored One with the five limbs touching the ground,” the preceding section clarified the departure from defilement and birth in purity; this section now distinguishes the causes for departing from defilement and being born in purity.
By what means can one leave behind defilement and be born into purity?
It is by cultivating the causes that one attains the departure from defilement and birth into purity.
Prostrating oneself with the five limbs touching the ground to seek compassion and repent is precisely the cause for departing from defilement and departing from evil.
"May the Buddha-Sun teach me to contemplate pure karma"—this clarifies the wholesome causes for birth in the Pure Land.
From "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards is the second section: the general response.

As for what is called the "general response," it refers to directly emitting light that transforms into golden pedestals, causing the pure lands of the ten directions to all appear therein, so that Lady Vaidehī may behold them all universally and be enabled to be reborn there according to her wish.
This is a general answer to the preceding question.
However, this answer differs from the preceding question: whereas the former question was posed through speech, the present answer is given by emitting light;
the former was addressed to the śrāvakas, while the present is an answer in terms of form.
"At that time, Vaidehī addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
These buddha-lands... Below this, the second section specifically elucidates the Pure Land.
The previous section posed general questions regarding the pure lands of the ten directions without specifying which particular land one wished to be reborn in; therefore, it was general.
This present section, however, specifically clarifies the Western Pure Land of Amitābha; therefore, it is specific.
In this context, the preceding section provided the answer to a question, whereas the present section poses that very question.
Question:
Since the Buddha universally manifests pure lands throughout the ten directions, for what reason do people aspire to be reborn specifically in the Western Land of Amitābha?
The commentary states:
According to what is analyzed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, among the pure lands of a million asaṃkhyeya chapters, Amitābha’s land in the West is the most inferior.
Since it is the lowest grade, for what reason does one vow to be reborn there?
The commentary states:
Having first abandoned the defiled for the pure, the remaining pure realms are not easily accessible.
For this reason, one can only attain rebirth in the Pure Land of the West.
"Then the World-Honored One smiled" marks the beginning of the second section: the specific response.
Within this specific response, there are two parts:
first, the emission of light to benefit King Bimbisāra;
Second, he next expounded the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land for Vaidehī.

Previously, by means of the wheel of supernatural power through the emission of light, he benefited his father, the King; subsequently, by expounding the Pure Land, he benefited Queen Vaidehī through the wheel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the previous emission of light brought minor benefit to the father-king, while the subsequent teaching on the Pure Land brings great benefit to the mother-queen.
Regarding the "minor benefit to the father-king," it means that the king had originally attained the first fruit of the path.
How is this known?
It is recorded in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "When the Prince left the city to study the Way, he arrived at the royal capital to seek alms from his attendants.
Countless people came to gaze upon the King."
The boy made a vow, saying:
"Before the Prince attains the Way, you must deliver me; please accept my invitation.
Later, when he had attained Buddhahood, the king led eighty-four thousand people to welcome the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* on the way.
Thus, having previously attained the first fruit, he now, through the illumination of the light, advanced to attain the stage of *anāgāmin*; therefore, this was his minor benefit.

The lady received great benefit; having heard the teaching of the Pure Land Dharma-gate, she attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and thus this was a great benefit.
This was King Śibi’s skillful means for benefiting his parents.
If one does not take parents as objects of attachment, by what means could a father sever the afflictions of the desire realm to attain the stage of Anāgāmin?
And by what means could a mother be born in a pure land and attain the patience of non-arising?
Since such benefits were obtained by means of this matter, we know it was a skillful expedient (*upāya*).
Furthermore, the previous emission of light benefited the father, which constitutes benefit in the present;
the subsequent preaching of the Dharma benefited the mother, which constitutes benefit for the future.
Regarding these two sections, each is further divided into two distinct parts.
In the first section, the first part is the actual exercise of the wheel of supernormal powers;
the second part is the father-king’s attainment of benefit.
Regarding the two parts of the latter section: first, the Tathāgata’s actual turning of the wheel of the Dharma;
second, the realization of benefit by the noble lady.
This [first part] is the Tathāgata’s actual exercise of the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*).
"From 'At that time, although the Great King was in confinement' onwards is the second [section], concerning the father king’s attainment of benefit, as per the text.
From 'At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vaidehī' onwards is the second [section], concerning the turning of the Wheel of Dharma to benefit the lady."
The "Great Opening" is divided into two parts as previously explained: first, the actual turning of the wheel of Dharma;
second, the benefits obtained by the ladies.
Within the section on the preaching of the Dharma, there are two further divisions:
First, it clarifies that the three kinds of goodness serve as the causes for the Pure Land;
second, it clarifies that the sixteen contemplations serve as the causes for the Pure Land.
Within these two chapters, there are further two aspects each:
First, the introduction;
second, the formal exposition of the three kinds of goodness as the causes for the Pure Land.
The latter two [sections] are likewise structured: first the introduction, followed by the formal exposition of the sixteen contemplations as the causes for the Pure Land.
Now, regarding the first dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
there are two parts herein:
first, the injunction to listen;
Second is the granting of the discourse.
Now, the instruction to listen is given as in the text:
"I shall now explain many parables for you in detail," which constitutes the granting of the discourse.
The passage beginning with "Also for the sake of future generations" clarifies the purpose of the teaching.
The reason it is taught is that one desires to benefit sentient beings of both the present and the future.
"Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three kinds of merit. Second, the correct exposition of the three types of goodness as the causes for the Pure Land.
This is divided into three parts:
the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
"One should cultivate the three blessings" is the heading.
From "First, filial support and nourishment" onwards is the second section, which explains the three blessings.
The explanation of the three blessings follows the text as it stands.
This clarifies these three types of meritorious goodness; these three categories encompass all such goodness without exception.
Why is this? The first is the mundane goodness of ordinary worldlings; the second is the goodness of the Hīnayāna; and the third is the goodness of the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, the first category consists of worldly ordinary persons who are virtuous; as the text states, they "filially support their parents and practice the ten wholesome actions," yet have not yet received the three refuges or the five precepts.

Second, before clearly explaining the reception of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, it first clarifies filial support for one's parents and the practice of the ten wholesome actions; therefore, we know these are the wholesome deeds of worldly ordinary persons, and they are also "old" wholesome deeds.
This goodness existed even before the Buddha was born; therefore, it is called "ancient goodness.
Second, the reception of the three refuges and the five precepts, up to the two hundred and fifty precepts and so forth—these are the "guest goodness" of the Buddha.
The virtues of the Hīnayāna begin with receiving the three refuges and culminate in the virtues of the ten precepts; therefore, these are the Hīnayāna virtues of the Buddha-dharma.
Third, generating the bodhicitta, believing in cause and effect, and reading and reciting Mahāyāna sūtras constitute the Mahāyāna virtues.

These three types encompass both the mundane and the supramundane; they encompass the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, and they exhaustively include all that is wholesome. Therefore, these three types are elucidated.
Yet, regarding these three kinds of goodness, one may possess them as three distinct persons, or one may possess them as a single person.
Regarding these three types of persons, they are as previously described.

As for obtaining even one such person: beginning from an ordinary being who spontaneously cultivates this goodness, then entering the Buddha-dharma to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and eventually proceeding from the Small Vehicle into the Mahāyāna—such a single individual, from beginning to end, fully cultivates these three forms of goodness.
Question:
These three kinds of goodness serve as the causes for pure lands; do they produce three distinct types of pure lands, or do they produce only one type of pure land?
Explanation:
There are three kinds of goodness that give rise to three kinds of pure lands:
superior goodness gives rise to a superior pure land, middling goodness gives rise to a middling pure land, and inferior goodness gives rise to an inferior pure land.
Originally, it was taught that three grades of goodness give rise to one pure land; now, herein it is clarified that these three kinds of goodness give rise to one pure land.
How is this known?
Since it is now clarified that these three kinds of goodness give rise to the Western Pure Land of Amitābha, we know that the three kinds of goodness give rise to a single type of land.
Question:
Since there are three kinds of wholesome causes, how can only one kind of pure land be produced?
Explanation:

Although these three types of beings are born together in the same pure land, their karmic rewards within that pure land differ; because their causes vary in depth, the fruits they attain also differ in degree of excellence.
Just as the sentient beings within this defiled land, though all dwelling together in a world of impurity, differ in their status— whether noble or base, ascending or sinking—
so too is it with those born in that land.
Question:
If one cultivates these three kinds of causes, how can one attain birth in the Pure Land?
Explanation:
These three types are all pure minds.
The mind that filially supports one's parents is also pure;
even the mind that resolves upon bodhicitta is also pure.
Because these three kinds of mind are all pure, the land attained is also pure.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti* says: "Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure."
If one attains this mind, this very mind is itself the Western Pure Land.
Why? Because both purity and defilement reside solely within the mind.
If the mind is pure, one perceives this land as pure.
Furthermore, if one attains the pure mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then there is the land of the ultimate truth.
Now, the land of the ultimate truth is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Dharma-body and the land of the ultimate truth are not different from one another.
The meaning of "a place where one may take refuge" is termed a "land" (*kṣetra*); that which has no response to stimuli is termed the "Dharmakāya.
Thus, the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "Those of the Three Worthies and Ten Sages dwell in the retribution [lands]; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land."
If one gives rise to afflictions and delusions, this is the defiled land of the three miserable realms;
if one commits the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, this is the Avīci Hell, where one's body is eighty thousand yojanas in height and breadth.
Therefore, both purity and defilement arise from the mind.
Herein, the three types of pure karma are clarified as the causes for birth in the Pure Land.
The passage beginning with "These three matters are called pure karma" constitutes the third section: the conclusion regarding the three types of karma.
As stated in the text:
"The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī," and so forth. Regarding the preceding clarification that the three kinds of goodness serve as the causes for the Pure Land, there are two parts:
first, the causal origin (*nidāna*); [second, the actual teaching].
Second, the explicit explanation of the three kinds of goodness as the cause for the Pure Land.
Now, secondly, the explanation of the sixteen kinds of contemplation as the cause for the Pure Land.
This also has two parts:
First, the introductory context;
second, the formal exposition of the sixteen kinds of contemplation, which constitutes the actual practice of the visualization of Amitāyus.
Now follows the introductory context.
There are seven points, which shall be identified in the text as they occur.
For now, the first is the exhortation to listen.
Question:
It was addressed to Vaidehī; why, then, was it also addressed to Ānanda?
The explanation is as follows:
it was addressed to Vaidehī to cause her to listen with single-minded attention.
He commanded Ānanda to propagate and transform those who have not yet heard [the Dharma].
For these reasons, he addressed both individuals together.
Regarding the phrase, "The Tathāgata now, for the sake of future generations," this is the second point, explaining the intent behind teaching pure karma.
With what intention is this pure karma taught?
It is for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages that this pure karma is taught.
"Excellent, Vaidehī," refers to the third [section], the praise of her inquiry.
Previously, the two were addressed together; now, the two are praised together.
The reason for praising Vaidehī’s question is that, because of her inquiry, she has presently attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), which accords with the Buddha’s mind.
Furthermore, because of her question, the palace ladies gave rise to the bodhicitta and further praised the Buddha’s mind.
Because they praised the Buddha’s mind, they extolled the question she had asked.
Furthermore, this question attains immediate benefit in the present and further augments that of the future.

Because it serves both self-benefit and the benefit of others, as well as benefit in the present and the future, for these reasons, he praised him, saying: "Excellent is this inquiry into such a matter."
"Ānanda, you should receive and uphold this," is the fourth [point], where the Buddha commands Ānanda to receive and uphold it so that he may transmit and transform future generations.
"The Buddha told Vaidehī, 'You are an ordinary person,'" is the fifth, where he addresses Vaidehī again.
This clarifies the Tathāgata’s skillful means, enabling Vaidehī to behold the Pure Land.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, Vaidehī addressed the Buddha," the sixth section follows: Vaidehī’s further inquiry.
The intent of this question is as follows: "I have now been able to see this land by means of the Buddha's power;
but after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how shall sentient beings be able to see it?
This is asked again for the sake of future sentient beings.
Regarding the term "five sufferings," these are like the five pains and five burnings described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, as they appear in that text.
Furthermore, they may also be identified as the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), for the five turbidities are designated as the five sufferings.
From "The Buddha addressed Vaidehī" onwards is the seventh section, which again addresses Vaidehī,
instructing her to focus her mind on the visualization of Amitāyus so that she may attain birth in that land.
From "How does one form the perception? onwards is the second section: the actual practice of the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*).
Within this, as there are sixteen contemplations in total, they should be divided into sixteen sections.
Now, this is divided into two parts:
first, thirteen contemplations for forming the visualization of Amitāyus;
second, three contemplations for forming the visualization of the nine grades.
Question:
Now, in contemplating Amitāyus, one should contemplate only Amitāyus.
For what reason does one contemplate the nine grades?
The commentary states:
The Contemplation of Immeasurable Life contemplates the fruit, while the contemplations of the nine grades contemplate the cause.
Because it contemplates both the cause and the fruit of the Pure Land, it is divided into two sections.
Regarding the first [section], the contemplation of Amitāyus is further divided into two parts:
first, six contemplations for observing the land of Amitāyus;
second, seven contemplations for observing the body of the Buddha Amitāyus.
One contemplates the trees and ponds within the Land of Immeasurable Life;
one contemplates the Buddha and the bodhisattvas within the presence of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
Furthermore, when contemplating the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, one is contemplating the fruit of the supporting environment.
To contemplate the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is to contemplate the world of the ultimate fruition;
furthermore, to contemplate the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is to contemplate the world of the pure land,
and to contemplate the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is to contemplate the world of perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the preceding contemplation of the Land of Immeasurable Life, there are further two points of intent:
first, five distinct contemplations;
second, one comprehensive contemplation.
Regarding the individual contemplations, one performs five distinct types of contemplation.

As for the sixth, the collective contemplation: because there are immeasurable matters in the Land of Immeasurable Life that cannot be contemplated in detail, the sixth contemplation collectively encompasses all of them.
Regarding the first [section], it is further divided into two:
first, one *pāda* and a half of contemplation as the preparatory means for contemplation;
second, three *pādas* and a half of contemplation as the actual practice of contemplation.
Now, first is the preparatory method for visualization.
Those who wish to perform the visualization of Amitāyus should face west and contemplate the sun with focused attention, causing the mind to become settled.
If one does not fixate the mind on the sun, the mind will not abide.
By fixing the mind and forming a mental image of the sun, the mind will attain abiding.
Because the mind abides, it naturally attains purity and beholds that land.
Next, one should cultivate the visualization of water.

As for why one first cultivated the visualization of the sun and now cultivates the visualization of water: because the light of the sun is radiant and pure, one first cultivated the visualization of the sun;
because water is transparent and clear, such that nothing is unseen, one now cultivates the visualization of water.
From the phrase "having formed the mental image" onwards is the second section: the actual practice of contemplation.
By forming the perception of water and the perception of lapis lazuli, one then sees that ground of lapis lazuli.
One sees the lapis lazuli ground, all of which is transparent and penetrating such that nothing is unseen.
The reason the ground was seen first is that the ground is its foundation; therefore, the ground was explained first.
Regarding the phrase "Below, there are vajra seven-jeweled banners supporting the ground," this is similar to the Lotus Treasury [World].
Why is it named the Lotus Treasury?
Because jewel lotuses support the world, it is therefore called the Lotus Treasury World.
In the western world, the world-realm known as Vajradhvaja-avalambana is called "Peaceful Bliss" (Anle) or "Ultimate Bliss" (Jile); these are merely different names for the same place.

This banner-like realm extends in all eight directions, composed of immeasurable various jewels, reflecting the colors of infinite radiance, and is adorned with various ornaments, such as lapis lazuli ground interspersed with gold.
As analyzed in the text, this is truly delightful.

Regarding the statement, "The Buddha told Ānanda, 'You must uphold the Buddha’s words,'" the three types of contemplation have been explained above; now, by commanding him to uphold them, the Buddha intends for them to be transmitted and propagated for future generations.
Question:
If the essence of the "good" were to be concluded upon the completion of each individual contemplation, or otherwise concluded all at once,
why is it concluded only upon reaching this point?
The commentary states:
Having reached the conclusion of these three contemplations, the matter does not exceed three; therefore, they are summarized following the three contemplations.
Furthermore, while the preceding section clarified the three contemplations, this section clarifies the essence of contemplation.
Now, the power and function of this contemplation are being distinguished.
What kind of power and function does performing this contemplation possess?

For this reason, it is now clarified that it can eliminate the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas, and that by casting off the body, one attains rebirth in a Pure Land.
Question:
Why is it that by contemplating earth, water, and so forth, one is able to eliminate a great many transgressions?
Furthermore, without performing confession, by what causes and conditions are such transgressions extinguished?
The commentary states:
Herein, one practices the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
Now, there are two kinds of *nien-fo san-mei*:
There are two types: the general and the specific.
Merely recollecting the Buddha is called the Specific Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi.

Recollecting the Buddha’s land, trees, and so forth, up to recollecting the Buddha’s attendants and so on—that is, recollecting both the primary and secondary aspects—is called the General Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi.
Question:
By what cause can the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) extinguish such a multitude of transgressions?
Explanation:
The Buddha possesses immeasurable merit; by recollecting the Buddha’s immeasurable merit, one is able to extinguish immeasurable transgressions.
Question:
One can extinguish transgressions by recollecting the Buddha’s primary fruition (the fruit of Buddhahood).
Now, one may wonder: since the earth and water are resultant fruits (*phala*), how can they eliminate transgressions?
The explanation is as follows:
these are the resultant fruits of the Buddha, produced by the Buddha’s untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
This tree is the Buddha-tree; its earth and water are the Buddha’s earth and water. To be mindful of the Buddha’s earth and water is to be mindful of the Buddha.
This earth and water is soft and subtle, unlike the earth and water here in this world.
Why is this? Even the precious objects of the heavens are said to communicate with one another; how much more so the land and water of the fruition-realm of Amitāyus Buddha?
This earth and water are subtle, wondrous, and pure, like a dream or an illusion.
The basis is not different from the correct, and the correct is not different from the basis.
The basis is correct while the incorrect is not the basis; the basis is correct while the non-basis is not the correct basis.
When the basis is correct, consciousness relies on the correct; when consciousness does not rely on the correct, it is through the provisional that consciousness is within [the correct].
If that is so, does this not mean that one extinguishes sin?
For the text says, "When one contemplates in accordance with this, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
By what intention is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas attained?

Because consciousness relies on what is correct and does not rely on what is incorrect, and because consciousness is provisionally awakened within the Middle Way, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

If one were merely to practice the visualization of the lapis lazuli ground and see a beautiful, pure ground, greed would arise; however, by contemplating whether it is the ground or not the ground, one thereby attains the extinction of offenses.
Therefore, the text says: "To observe in this way is called right observation; to observe in any other way is called wrong observation.
Question: According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, why is it that by observing earth, water, and so forth, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
"You have realized the realm of ultimate truth and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Furthermore, because you perceive emptiness, you have severed the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Now, when observing earth, water, and so forth, how do you sever delusions and attain non-arising?"

What is clarified here is as follows: as previously observed, this earth and water are like a dream and like an illusion; because they exist in the manner of a dream and an illusion, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
From "The Buddha said to Ānanda" onwards, the preceding section has concluded the explanation of the three contemplations; now, fourthly, is the contemplation of the jewel-trees.
This text is easy to understand.
Regarding the distinction between the pure land elucidated in this sutra and that elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* explains the pure land in two places.
First, in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa," the defiled is transformed into a pure land;
second, in the "Chapter on the Lifespan," the assembly perceives the world being consumed by fire, yet my pure land is not destroyed;
and third, the present Western Pure Land—these three passages constitute the meaning of these three phrases.
When the multitude sees them all consumed by fire while my Pure Land remains undestroyed, then two substances occupy one place;
when the defiled is transformed into a Pure Land, then one substance occupies one place.
Now, when the Pure Land is manifested, there are two substances and two locations.

To say that my Pure Land is not destroyed while having two substances and one location means that the Pure Vulture Peak exists within the site of the Impure Vulture Peak; thus, the impure and the pure do not obstruct one another.
Yet, while the defiled substance is burned, the pure substance is not destroyed;
therefore, these two substances occupy the same location.

That the defiled is transformed into the pure within a single substance and a single location means simply that the defiled substance is transformed into a pure substance, just as stone is transformed into jade or earth is transformed into gold.
Just as earth and stone are transformed into gold and jade, so too is soil;
likewise, when the environment is now transformed into purity or defilement, it occurs within this very same place. Therefore, it is a single substance and a single location.
This passage clarifies the two natures and two locations of the Pure Land: the purity of the Western region and the defilement of the Eastern land constitute the two natures;
the pure nature resides in the location of the West, while the defiled nature resides in the location of the East.
Therefore, these two consist of two substances and two locations.
Since the earth possesses these three phrases, does humanity also possess these three phrases?
The explanation says:
There are also those who speak of three propositions regarding persons.
As for "two substances and one location," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "I and the assembly of monks together depart from Vulture Peak Mountain."
The assembly of monks consists of virtuous people, while the rest of the multitude consists of defiled people.
The rest of the multitude burns themselves, but those within the assembly of monks are not burned.
These two groups—the pure and the defiled—reside together on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa without obstructing one another.

Just as the impurity of a Śūdra deity does not obstruct its purity, so it is with these two individuals—one pure and one impure—who may occupy the same place without mutual obstruction; therefore, these two substances coexist in a single location.

Regarding "two substances and two places": this refers to moving all devas and humans and placing them in other lands, such that pure beings are situated in pure places and defiled beings are situated in defiled places; therefore, these are called the two substances and two places.
Regarding "a single substance in a single location": it is just as when clouds transform a defiled land into a pure land—a single substance in a single location.

Now, when a śrāvaka transforms into a bodhisattva, both were previously śrāvakas; now, returning to the Mahāyāna and becoming a bodhisattva occurs right here. Therefore, it is a single substance in a single location.
Next, one should contemplate water; this is the fifth, the contemplation of water.
Question:
Since the contemplation of water has already been completed previously, for what reason is water contemplated again now?
The commentary states:
The previous contemplation of water was the preparatory skillful means; within that visualization of water, one contemplated the earth, the trees, and the water.

Now, one contemplates that pond-water, which is endowed with the eight meritorious qualities and adorned with various jewels, where the water produces the five musical tones and the birds praise the Triple Gem.
This is as stated in the text.
Regarding the passage "Upon each world-realm of the land of many jewels" and below: previously, there was a separate contemplation; now, this is the second, a collective contemplation.
Since the separate contemplations have not yet been fully discussed, they are now collectively contemplated.

Regarding the phrase, "If one sees this, the heavy evil karma of immeasurable kalpas is eliminated": previously, the essence of contemplation was clarified; now, the function of contemplation is clarified.
There are two categories of the six contemplations:
the first three clarify the essence of contemplation, while the subsequent three clarify the function of contemplation.
Now it is the same here: first the essence of the three contemplations was clarified, and next their function was clarified.
The previous three contemplations were still shallow, as they merely extinguish the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
"Now, as one contemplates this, it becomes ever deeper, capable of extinguishing immeasurable billions of kalpas of extremely grave evil offenses.
From "The Buddha told Ānanda" onwards, the text correctly presents the contemplation of the fruit.
The middle section consists of two parts:
first, the conclusion of the contemplation on the consequential fruit;
second, from "Now this" onwards, the contemplation on the primary fruit.
Previously, there were two types of contemplation based on the fruit:
first, contemplation of the preparatory means; second, contemplation of the essential body.
Now, the contemplation of the essential body of the actual fruit likewise has two parts:
The first clarifies the preparatory methods for contemplation (*vipaśyanā-vidhi*), and the second distinguishes the essential body of contemplation.
Now, regarding the first—the preparatory methods for contemplation—it is further divided into four parts;
this is the first: the admonition to listen and the permission to speak.
As stated in the text:
"You all should remember and uphold this" marks the second section, which commands the transmission of the teaching to future generations.
"When these words were spoken, Amitāyus Buddha stood in mid-air" marks the third section, in which Amitāyus Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas appear before Vaidehī.
The reason why the Buddha and Bodhisattvas appear before that person is so that they may serve as the objects of contemplation.

Since that person intends to perform the visualization of Amitāyus Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas, the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas therefore manifest before that person to serve as the objective field for their visualization.

From the passage "At that time, Vaidehī saw... onwards is the fourth section: because Vaidehī beheld the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas, she subsequently practiced the contemplations of Amitāyus Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas for the sake of future sentient beings.
From "The Buddha said to Vaidehī" onwards is the second section, which correctly elucidates the essence of the contemplations (*vipaśyanā*).
This is divided into two parts according to the text:
first, the individual contemplations; [and second, the general contemplation].
Second, the general contemplation.
Within the preceding contemplation on the fruit, there are two parts:
first, the specific contemplation; [second, the general contemplation].
Second, the general contemplation (*sāmānyālambana*).
Now, the contemplation of the actual fruit is likewise twofold: first, the specific contemplation (*viśeṣālambana*), and second, the general contemplation.
Regarding these terms "general" and "specific": contemplating the single body of Amitāyus and contemplating the single bodies of the two Bodhisattvas constitutes the specific contemplation.
Amitāyus possesses an inconceivable body, and the two Bodhisattvas are likewise so.
To contemplate the immeasurable bodies of Amitāyus and the two Bodhisattvas constitutes the general contemplation.
Within the first section on individual contemplation, there are further two parts:
first, the practice of imaginative visualization;
second, the practice of the true observation.
The reason for previously practicing the visualization of the image is that the marks of the immeasurable bodies are inconceivable.
Since the image is as if situated in space and cannot be constructed, one previously practiced the visualization of the image.
First one practices the visualization of the sixteen-foot body, followed by the visualization of the hundred-foot body; this is called the contemplation of the image-conception (*nimitta-saṃjñā*).
Because one has previously practiced the contemplation of the image-conception, one subsequently performs the true contemplation of the Buddha-body.
Question:
One first performs the contemplation of mental imagery and subsequently performs the contemplation of reality; can these be considered the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本)?
Explanation:

If one wishes to practice this path, it may be taken as having the preceding contemplation of mental images (*xiangxiang guan*) as its trace and the subsequent true contemplation (*zhen guan*) as its basis;
yet, while this may be done, such a designation is not convenient.
It is simply that one first performs the visualization of mental imagery and subsequently performs the visualization of reality.
Within the initial visualization of mental imagery, there are two parts:
first, visualizing the lotus pedestal of that Buddha;
Second, visualize that Buddha together with the two Bodhisattvas.
Within the visualization of the lotus pedestal, there are three parts:
first, the correct visualization of the lotus pedestal;
Second, explaining the causes of the flower pedestal;
third, explaining the efficacy of the contemplation of mental imagery.
Now, this is the first: the actual visualization of the flower pedestal.
This is as stated in the text.
From the passage "Ānanda, this flower pedestal" onwards, the second section clarifies the causes of the flower pedestal.
This flower pedestal was accomplished through the power of the original vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara; thus, it clarifies the fundamental cause of the pedestal.
"Once this visualization is accomplished, it eliminates [defilements]"—the following section is third, clarifying the efficacy of the contemplation of the provisional image.
As the text states.
"The Buddha told Ānanda"—the following section is second, visualizing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are two [aspects]:
first, visualizing the Dharma-body Buddha;
second, visualizing the Response-body Buddha.
Now, first of all, one should contemplate the Buddha of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding the Buddha of the Dharma-body, the text states: "The Tathāgata is the body of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)," which is precisely the Dharma-body.
All things are the Dharma-realm, and all things are the Dharma-body; therefore, one first forms this contemplation. Next, it says:
"This mind is itself the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; this mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Thus, there are three [points].
The reason for clarifying these three is to show that these three meanings are complete within this mind.
This mind is itself the thirty-two marks; it is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This mind is Buddha; it is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
That "this mind creates the Buddha" clarifies the cause of the two bodies (dvayakāya).
Now, let us ask the Sāṃkhya teacher:
how do you explain that this mind is the Buddha?
"Are the thirty-two marks the mind that is itself Buddha?
He replied:
"That the mind is itself Buddha—this is the ultimate truth."
Otherwise, if ultimate truth were a dull state devoid of cognition, how could it be the Buddha?
The Buddha is defined as "awakened," therefore ultimate truth is not the Buddha.
Furthermore, since ultimate truth is without mind and without Buddha, how can one say that the mind is the truth?
Furthermore, the mind is mind, while the thirty-two marks are form; how could mind and form possibly be identical?
If you claim they are identical to reality, that is also not the case.
In identity with reality, there is neither mind nor form; therefore, identity cannot be established.
If it were conventional truth (*saṃvṻti-satya*), then one could not attain immediate realization;
thus, the two phrases would remain unintelligible.

At that time, the unimpeded mind is itself the Buddha. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three have no different characteristics. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa do not differ by even a hair’s breadth. And the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Contemplate the true reality of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way."
It is the same now: the mind itself is the Buddha, and the Buddha himself is the mind.
If this mind is perfected, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is perfected.
Once the Dharma-body is perfected, the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is likewise perfected.
Therefore, the mind is this, and the thirty-two marks are this; this is precisely the Buddha.
"For this reason, one should be single-minded" and below, the second [section] concerns the visualization of the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) Buddha.
The mind as it was previously cultivated is itself the Buddha. If this contemplation is perfected, there is no need to perform this contemplation again. Why?
Because the mind is itself the Buddha.
However, for those of dull faculties, what is established is not [correct]; now, in order to cause them to recognize what is incorrect, it is necessary to perform this contemplation.
Yet, there are times when both are eliminated, and there are times when one clarifies that they are identical.
Regarding the simultaneous removal [of both]: there has never been a Buddha apart from the mind, for it is by virtue of the mind that there is a Buddha.
Since the mind is ultimately unattainable, the Buddha is likewise unattainable.
This is not the ultimate truth.
Although it is neither mind nor Buddha, this is precisely great wisdom.
To say that "action is itself contemplation" clarifies that the mind is itself the Buddha.
Since this is the case for contemplating the mind, it is likewise so for contemplating the Buddha.
Since these two contemplations are both insufficient, one is further instructed to perform the contemplation of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
This latter section consists of three parts;
the first is the visualization of the Buddha.
Second, visualize the two Bodhisattvas;
third, clarify the power and function of contemplation.
This constitutes the first [section]: visualizing the body of that Buddha.
As analyzed in the text:
"Furthermore, one should again perform... and so forth. Second, the visualization of the two bodhisattvas.
First, one visualizes the two lotus seats; next, one visualizes the two bodhisattvas, as described in the text.
However, this perception purifies the mind; when the mind is purified, the Buddha-field is purified. The Buddha-field arises solely from the mind:

because the mind is defiled, the Buddha-field is defiled; because the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure. Because there are one million varieties of mind, there are one million varieties of pure lands.
Because the Buddha’s mind is foremost in purity, his buddha-field is foremost in purity; thus it is said, "Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
Regarding the passage beginning with "One who practices this contemplation," the third section clarifies the efficacy of this contemplation.
As contemplation becomes progressively deeper, the effort required consequently increases.

In the passage beginning with "The Buddha told Ānanda: Once this visualization is accomplished, next one should... and so forth, the previous section on the specific contemplations for the primary fruit was originally divided into two parts; the first, the contemplation of mental imagery, is now concluded.
Now, secondly, one performs the visualization of reality (*bhūta-darśana*). These two visualizations are both performed within the context of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

While the preceding was the visualization of the response-body through mental imagery, this present visualization of the response-body is the visualization of the true body (*dharmakāya*) of Amitāyus Buddha.
This consists of three parts:
first, the visualization of Amitāyus Buddha;
second, the visualization of Avalokiteśvara.
Third, one contemplates Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Now, first, one contemplates the body of Amitāyus Buddha;
the phrases and sentences herein are easily understood.

However, while Śākyamuni possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, that Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks, and each mark has eighty-four thousand minor characteristics.

When Śākyamuni was a prince, his *ūrṇā* (white tuft of hair) was five feet long; after he attained Buddhahood, it became fifteen feet long when extended, but when released, it would retract and become like a conch shell.
The white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of that Buddha curls to the right like five Mount Sumerus.
Furthermore, the physical marks of that Buddha’s body fill the entirety of space, and his entire assembly likewise fills the entirety of space.
The reason for these differences is that they are all perceived according to the specific conditions encountered.

Regarding the statement, "One who practices this contemplation attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)," one might ask: while now contemplating the Buddha’s body and its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), how can one attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena?
This has already been explained previously;
now I shall provide another interpretation.
It clarifies that this very state is itself non-arising (*anutpāda*); why then must one further seek to realize the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
If even Master Dafeng attained the realization of non-arising upon hearing a dog bark, how much more so should one attain non-arising by now contemplating the body of the Buddha?
"The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī" refers to the second contemplation: the contemplation of the body of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, as described in the text.
Next, thirdly, one contemplates the body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
These two contemplations each possess both a primary essence and a functional application, as can be understood from the text.

From the passage "When seeing this matter, one should give rise to the thought that one is born in the Western Land" onwards, within the contemplation of the primary fruit, there are originally two parts; the first, the individual contemplation, is now concluded.
Now, secondly, the general contemplation.
Within this text, there are two types of contemplation:
first, the universal contemplation; [second, the specific contemplation].
Second is the Contemplation of Mixture.

Regarding the term "Universal Contemplation" (Puguān): it refers to contemplating in their entirety the body of Amitāyus Buddha, his retinue, and his teachings; hence it is called Universal Contemplation.

Regarding what is called "mixed contemplation": it refers to contemplating either the complete body of Amitāyus, or his transformation bodies—whether large or small—as well as the entire bodies of the two bodhisattvas.
Because one contemplates the various bodies and teachings of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is called "contemplating the miscellaneous" (zaguān).
Now, however, it is first the "universal contemplation" (puguān),
as the text states.
Below "The Transformation Body of Amitāyus Buddha," the second section concerns miscellaneous visualizations.
Below "The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī regarding the superior grade," the sixteen chapters on visualization are broadly divided into two sections:
first, thirteen visualizations that observe the fruition;
Second, there are three contemplations for observing the cause.
Having completed the observation of the fruit, one now observes the cause.
As for "observing the fruit," it refers to observing the two fruits—the environment and the inhabitants—of Amitāyus Buddha; hence, it is called "observing the fruit."
Regarding the contemplation of causes, there are three grades of rebirth.
If one asks what constitutes this contemplation for the three grades of rebirth,
the explanation is as follows:
These three grades are the causes for birth in the Pure Land.
Now, observing that there are superior, middling, and inferior causes for birth in the Pure Land, it is therefore called "contemplation" (guan).
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* explains only three grades, whereas here the three grades are further divided into nine grades.
The three grades refer to the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
Regarding the nine grades: there are three in the superior grade, and likewise three in the middle and inferior grades; thus, they constitute nine grades.
The present case refers to the first [of these], which comprises the three within the superior grade.

The previous section explained the highest grade of birth: by generating the bodhicitta and practicing for seven days, one will be born in that land, behold the body of that Buddha, hear the preaching of the wondrous Dharma, and thereby realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Question:
To what stage does this "non-arising" (anutpāda) belong?
Explanation:
This is the non-arising of the seventh stage. How is this known?
The explanation says:
The lower grade gives rise to the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and one attains the Stage of Joy.
Since the lower grade has already attained joy, one should know that this is the non-arising of the seventh stage.
Question:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains the practices of one bhūmi over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Now, in which bhūmi does one behold the body of Amitāyus Buddha and, upon hearing his Dharma, attain the realization of non-arising?
The commentary states:
This matter is difficult to know.

If one were to discuss it in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), this refers to a Bodhisattva of the sixth stage who, upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, attains the non-arising [wisdom] of the seventh stage.
Furthermore, there are those who transcend [the sequence of practice], such as Śākyamuni, who attained Buddhahood before Maitreya;

therefore, this cannot be known [by ordinary calculation]. Regarding "those of the highest grade who are born by middle capacity": second, this clarifies the person of the highest grade who is born by middle capacity. They do not necessarily recite Mahāyāna sūtras, but they skillfully understand the principles of the meaning, have deep faith in cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahāyāna. By virtue of these merits, they vow to be born in that land and immediately attain rebirth within a great precious lotus flower in the pool of seven treasures in that land; after one night has passed, the flower opens.
Nevertheless, even that single night is exceedingly long.
Why? Because one day and night there is equivalent to one *kalpa* in Jambudvīpa; thus, passing a single night there is equivalent to half a *kalpa* here.
After seven days, one does not regress from *samyak-saṃbodhi*; after one small kalpa, one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
One day and night there corresponds to one kalpa here; one kalpa there corresponds to immeasurable kalpas in this world.
This is also the non-arising of the seventh stage.
Previously, one attained non-arising by seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma at the superior level; now, at the middling level, one attains non-arising after the passing of a single small kalpa.
Regarding "the lower birth of the highest grade": third, this clarifies the lower birth of the highest grade.

This person also believes in cause and effect and does not slander the Mahāyāna; the lotus flower in that land blooms after one day and one night, and after further passing through three minor kalpas, they attain the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas and dwell on the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Now, since the lower grade attains the non-arising of the first stage (*bhūmi*), we know that the aforementioned upper grade refers to the non-arising of the seventh stage.
The reason for clarifying these two types of non-arising is that there are two locations for non-arising:
first, the non-arising of the first stage; [and second, the non-arising of the seventh stage].
Second, regarding the non-arising of the seventh stage: for this reason, the two kinds of non-arising are clarified.
Next, the rebirth of the three grades of the middle class is explained.
Among these, those who attain rebirth through the three grades all obtain the fruits of the Hīnayāna.
Those of the superior-middle grade of rebirth maintain the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the full set of precepts, and attain the fruit of Arhatship.

Those of the middle-middle grade maintain the eight precepts for one day and night, the śrāmaṇera precepts for one day and night, and the full set of precepts; they initially attain the fruit of Srotāpanna and, after half a kalpa, achieve the fruit of Arhatship.
Question:
While the eight precepts may be observed for one day and one night, how can the śrāmaṇera precepts and the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) precepts be observed for only one day and one night?
Explanation:

Regarding the phrase "one day and one night," this does not mean that one maintains the śrāmaṇera precepts or the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) for only a single day and night; rather, it refers to the case where one receives them for a day and a night and then dies, which is why it is called "one day and one night."
Those of the middle grade, lower level, shall attain the state of Arhat after the passing of one small kalpa.
Next, the rebirths of the three grades of the lower grade are explained; these are all of the Mahāyāna.
The first category attains the first stage (*bhūmi*); the middle category gives rise to the bodhicitta; and the lower category likewise possesses the bodhicitta.
However, these three categories are extremely difficult to understand, as there are briefly two points of doubt.
First, that the three individuals of the superior category attain the fruit of the Mahāyāna—of this there is no doubt.

Regarding the doubt concerning the latter two chapters: for what reason do the three persons of the middle grade attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), while the three persons of the lower grade attain the fruits of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*)?
It is because those of the middle grade attain the fruit of Arhatship, whereas those of the lower grade, conversely, attain the fruit of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) of the Great Vehicle.
Second, the sequence should not be as it is here.
For what reason are the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna not presented together in one place, with the Hīnayāna following the Mahāyāna, instead of first clarifying the Mahāyāna and then the Hīnayāna,
and having clarified the Hīnayāna, subsequently clarifying the Mahāyāna again?
The commentary states:
Since the attainment of the fruit occurs later, it ought to be placed at the end.
Furthermore, the current explanation regarding rebirth for the three grades of practitioners is based specifically on present causes and does not refer to the attainment of the fruit.
There are three grades of superiority and inferiority regarding present causes:
the first grade is to cultivate the goodness of the Mahāyāna and refrain from committing evil;
the second grade is to cultivate the goodness of the Hīnayāna and likewise refrain from committing evil.
The third category consists of those who do not cultivate goodness but instead commit evil.

Taking Mahāyāna goodness as the superior grade, Hīnayāna goodness as the middling grade, and sentient beings who commit evil and lack goodness as the inferior grade—these are the three grades established according to this principle.

Next, as to the question of why the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are explained in an intermingled manner rather than being placed together in one section and the Hīnayāna in another: this is also as answered previously; it is not that the sequence is established according to the attainment of the fruit, but merely refers to the priority and posteriority in terms of cultivation.
First, the goodness of the Mahāyāna is explained; next, the goodness of the Hīnayāna is explained; and finally, the state of having evil but no goodness is explained.
Thus, goodness is explained first and evil is explained last.
Within the section on goodness, the goodness of the Mahāyāna is explained first and the goodness of the Hīnayāna is explained afterward.
The "good" explained previously refers to the good of the five vehicles:
superior grade is the good of the Mahāyāna;
middle grade is the good of the Śrāvakas, humans, and devas.
The observance of the eight precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, the full ordination (upasaṃpadā), and so forth, constitutes the goodness of the Three Vehicles;
filial piety toward one’s parents and the practice of worldly benevolence constitute the goodness of humans and devas.
This clearly elucidates the full meaning of goodness.
Question:
Once the clarity regarding good is exhausted, is the clarity regarding evil also exhausted?
Explanation:
The third chapter clarifies that there are three types of persons who commit evil:
first, it clarifies those who commit the ten unwholesome deeds; next, it clarifies those who commit the four grave offenses; and finally, it clarifies those who commit the five heinous crimes.
Because it does not clarify those who slander the Dharma or the icchantikas, its explanation of evil is not exhaustive.

Those who have committed the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, or the five rebellious acts can all be reborn in the Western Land; however, those who slander the Dharma and are icchantikas cannot be reborn there.

The reason why those who slander the Dharma and are icchantikas cannot be reborn is that icchantikas do not believe in the Dharma; even if they are told of the presence of Amitāyus Buddha at the moment of death, they ultimately do not believe it, and therefore they cannot attain rebirth.

Furthermore, the same applies to the slander of the Dharma: for instance, when followers of the Hīnayāna hear it said that there are Buddhas in the ten directions, they do not believe it and therefore cannot attain rebirth there.
Because the causes cultivated in the present life vary in degree of excellence or inferiority, it is said that there are three distinct grades.
Question:
What is the purpose of cultivating [the path] in such a way as to attain these fruits?

While there are degrees of depth in the causes that manifest differences in the attainment of fruits, it has not yet been clarified what the intention behind the superior grade attaining the fruit of the Mahāyāna, the middling grade attaining the fruit of the Hīnayāna, and the inferior grade attaining the fruit of the Mahāyāna is.
The commentary states:
Because one pursues their respective causes of cultivation, the fruits obtained vary in magnitude.
By cultivating the superior grade of Mahāyāna causes, one consequently obtains the fruit of Mahāyāna.
Those of middling capacity cultivate the causes of the Hīnayāna, and therefore obtain the fruits of the Hīnayāna;

those of inferior capacity, although they do not currently cultivate Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna virtues, encounter a spiritual friend at the time of death who expounds the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna for them, and because they hear the Mahāyāna, they obtain the fruits of the Mahāyāna.

Those of superior grade have strong roots of goodness and strong fruits; those of middling grade have strong roots of goodness but weak fruits; those of inferior grade have weak roots of goodness but strong fruits.
Those of superior grade who cultivate the goodness of the Mahāyāna obtain the fruit of the Mahāyāna; their roots of goodness are strong and their fruits are likewise strong.

Those of middle capacity have strong roots of goodness but weak fruits: they practice the prohibitive precepts and worldly virtues to attain the fruits of the Hīnayāna; therefore, their goodness is strong while their fruits are weak.

Regarding "inferior-grade goodness with weak roots but strong fruits": this refers to individuals of inferior grade who do not cultivate goodness at all yet obtain great fruits; thus, their goodness is weak while their fruits are strong.

Furthermore, the reason those of inferior grade obtain great fruits is to clarify that although they do not cultivate goodness in the present, they may have previously awakened the aspiration [for enlightenment], or having now heard the Mahāyāna, they again awaken the aspiration, and so forth.
From the phrase "When these words were spoken" onwards, the main exposition is divided into two parts:
first, the benefit to the father king through the wheel of supernormal powers;
second, the benefit to the queen through the wheel of the Dharma.
Regarding the benefit of the Father King through the Wheel of Supernormal Powers, there are two parts:
first, the emission of light to illuminate the Father King;
second, the Father King’s attainment of benefit.
The benefits for the Lady when the Wheel of Dharma is taught also consist of two parts:
first, the actual teaching of the Dharma to the lady; second, the benefits obtained by the lady and her retinue.
The formal exposition has concluded; now follows the second section, on the benefits obtained by the lady, as per the text.
From "At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat" onwards is the third major section: the dissemination (*pravartana*).
The meaning of these phrases can be understood from the text itself.
Herein, there should be two points:
first, the entrustment for circulation within the palace; [and second, the entrustment for circulation outside the palace].
Second, after the Buddha returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, Ānanda again preached it for its circulation.
This concludes the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.
